titre: Triple Divide Peak, the ridge where a raindrop picks its ocean, or doesn't
accroche: A Montana peak sends water to three oceans. But another, 200 km away, claims the same title.
contenu_vulgarise:
At the top of a ridge in Montana, at 2,446 meters (8,025 feet) in elevation, a raindrop has only a few centimeters to decide its fate: depending on which side it lands on, it will reach the Pacific, the Gulf of Mexico, or Hudson Bay. Triple Divide Peak, in Glacier National Park, has been billed for decades as the only point in North America where water splits among three distinct oceans. Hydrographers, however, don't quite agree.

## The mechanism

The geography of the place is not in dispute. On the southwest slope of Triple Divide Peak, meltwater runs into Pacific Creek, then Nyack Creek, then the Middle Fork of the Flathead River, which ends up in the Columbia River and the Pacific Ocean, near Astoria (Oregon). On the southeast slope, it feeds Atlantic Creek, which joins the Missouri and then the Mississippi, headed for the Gulf of Mexico. On the north slope, it flows into Hudson Bay Creek, then Medicine Owl Creek, then Red Eagle Creek, before crossing Saint Mary Lake and the Saskatchewan River system to Hudson Bay. Three creeks, three basins, one ridge: the peak marks the meeting of the Continental Divide with the so-called “Laurentian” divide, or Northern Divide.

## The shift

The disagreement begins where hydrography ends and the mapping of oceans begins. Hudson Bay has no unambiguous international status: some classifications attach it to the Atlantic, others to the Arctic, and the International Hydrographic Organization leans toward the Arctic in a working edition that was never formally adopted. If Hudson Bay counts as an Arctic arm, then Triple Divide Peak does touch three distinct oceans (Pacific, Atlantic, Arctic) and deserves its title. But if it is placed on the Atlantic side, its other two basins, Mississippi and Saskatchewan-Nelson, both end up in the Atlantic: Triple Divide Peak then separates only two oceans, and the true triple point moves more than 200 kilometers away, to a glacial dome called Snow Dome, on the border of Alberta and British Columbia. Snow Dome does send its water to the Pacific via the Columbia River, to the Arctic via the Mackenzie River, and to Hudson Bay via the Nelson River: three directions that, in turn, only fail to overlap if Hudson Bay is counted as Atlantic.

The title of North America's “triple point of three oceans” therefore depends not on a measurement that could be refined in the field, but on a convention no authority has definitively settled: depending on which atlas you open, the same mountain loses or gains an ocean, and the peak that officially bears the name “Triple Divide” may not be the one that truly separates three oceans.

repere.texte: On this Montana peak, meltwater splits into three named creeks: Pacific Creek toward the Pacific Ocean via the Columbia River, Atlantic Creek toward the Mississippi and the Gulf of Mexico, and Hudson Bay Creek toward Hudson Bay via the Saskatchewan River system.

carte.punch: A Montana peak sends water to three oceans, unless a single bay is classified differently.
carte.idee: On Triple Divide Peak (Montana), three named creeks run toward the Pacific, the Gulf of Mexico, and Hudson Bay. But depending on whether Hudson Bay is classified as Atlantic or Arctic, the true triple point of the oceans shifts to another peak, Snow Dome, 200 km away.

quiz.question: Why do hydrographers dispute the status of Triple Divide Peak (Montana) as a “triple point of three oceans”?
choix: Because one of the three streams attributed to it dries up completely for part of the year
Because the exact course of the water divide has changed since the last geological survey
Because its status depends on a contested classification of Hudson Bay, which moves the triple point to Snow Dome
Because the peak actually straddles the border between Canada and the United States
quiz.explication: The controversy is not about the hydrography on the ground, which is well documented by three named creeks, but about a convention for classifying seas: if Hudson Bay is counted as an arm of the Atlantic, Snow Dome, in Alberta, becomes the true triple point; if it is counted as Arctic, Triple Divide Peak is. The International Hydrographic Organization has not settled the question officially.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Which stream, on the north slope of Triple Divide Peak, carries water to Hudson Bay?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The card names Hudson Bay Creek, on the north slope, as the first link in the route to Hudson Bay, via Medicine Owl Creek, Red Eagle Creek, and then the Saskatchewan system.

quiz_supplementaire.question: To which oceans or basins does Snow Dome, the rival peak 200 km from Triple Divide Peak, send its water?
choix: Pacific, Gulf of Mexico, and Hudson Bay
Atlantic, Arctic, and Gulf of Mexico
Only to the Pacific and the Atlantic
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The card states that Snow Dome sends its water to the Pacific via the Columbia, to the Arctic via the Mackenzie, and to Hudson Bay via the Nelson River.
